lesson.title: Packets Inside Packets: Crossing IPv4-Only Ground with a Tunnel
lesson.summary: Tunneling wraps one protocol's packets inside another protocol's packets so IPv6 traffic can cross networks that only understand IPv4, letting isolated IPv6 islands reach each other over IPv4-only infrastructure without every router in between needing an upgrade.
lesson.body:
Tunneling was named earlier as the second core strategy for bridging IPv4 and IPv6, and it solves a problem dual stack cannot: what happens when a device or network genuinely does support both protocols, but the path between it and another dual-stack-capable network runs through infrastructure that only understands IPv4. Rather than waiting for every router along that path to be upgraded, tunneling takes a complete IPv6 packet, header and payload together, and encapsulates the entire thing inside the payload portion of an IPv4 packet. To every IPv4 router along the way, this looks like an ordinary IPv4 packet, since only the outer IPv4 header is examined for forwarding decisions; the IPv6 packet riding inside is invisible to them and simply comes along for the ride as opaque payload data.

The encapsulation and decapsulation happen at the two ends of the tunnel, which are IPv6-and-IPv4-capable devices, typically routers, configured specifically to know that this tunnel exists. The entry point router takes the outbound IPv6 packet, wraps it inside a new IPv4 header addressed to the tunnel's far-end router, and sends it across the IPv4-only network in between. The exit point router receives that IPv4 packet, strips off the outer IPv4 header, and forwards the original, now-unwrapped IPv6 packet onward natively into IPv6 territory on the far side. From the perspective of the original sender and the ultimate IPv6 destination, the tunnel is invisible; it behaves like a single logical IPv6 hop even though several real IPv4 hops sit underneath it.

Several concrete tunneling mechanisms have been used at different points in the IPv6 transition. 6to4 automatically derives a globally routable IPv6 prefix from a device's public IPv4 address, embedding that IPv4 address inside the IPv6 prefix itself using the 2002 double-colon slash 16 block, and relies on relay routers to bridge between the 6to4 IPv6 space and native IPv6 networks. Teredo takes a similar approach but is specifically designed to work even when the local IPv4 address is hidden behind NAT, encapsulating IPv6 inside UDP inside IPv4 so it can traverse typical home routers. 6in4 is a simpler, manually configured point-to-point tunnel, often used by smaller organizations to get native-feeling IPv6 connectivity from a provider that offers only a tunnel broker service rather than native IPv6 on the local link.

Tunneling's overhead is the direct tradeoff for its flexibility: every tunneled packet carries two full headers, the outer IPv4 header and the inner IPv6 header, increasing the total bytes sent per packet and sometimes forcing fragmentation if the combined size exceeds the path's maximum transmission unit. It also adds a processing step, encapsulation and decapsulation, at both tunnel endpoints that a purely native dual-stack path never has to perform.

Because of that overhead, tunneling has always been treated as a bridge technique for specific gaps rather than a permanent architecture: as more of the underlying network infrastructure becomes natively dual-stack capable, the need for a given tunnel disappears, and traffic that once had to be wrapped and unwrapped can instead travel as plain, native IPv6 the whole way, which is the same end state dual stack was already providing wherever it was available.
